name: MATHia
line: MATHia tutors each step inside workspaces a teacher assigns. In AMP, every answer sets the next problem.
description: AMP vs MATHia: MATHia tutors each step in workspaces a teacher assigns. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous, at every problem.
verdict: MATHia tutors each step of a problem inside workspaces a teacher assigns, and the teacher decides what comes next [1]. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous. Every answer updates the learner's level and sets the next problem, and each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer.

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, everything hangs off the problem in front of the learner: a hint that gives the first step and never the answer, a written lesson with a worked example, a video lesson, the worked answer after it is answered, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. MATHia's unit is the workspace, a set of real problems, with a Skillometer showing progress [1]. In the course its evidence comes from, students advanced as they mastered skills [7].

reasons.title: Teaching at every problem
reasons.body: AMP's teaching sits at the problem, so the adult does not plan, teach or grade. After every answer the learner sees whether it was right, the correct answer and the worked steps. MATHia is built to work alongside core instruction, and its hints respond to the student's strategy [1]. In the course its evidence comes from, classes spent three days a week with a teacher and textbook and two on the software [7]. A meta-analysis of 55 studies found that worked examples improve math performance [12].

reasons.title: Every answer sets the next problem
reasons.body: AMP places a learner from their first answers. Every answer after that updates the learner's level and sets the next problem: new work within reach, a gap to close, or an old skill due back. Repeated misses send practice back to what the skill builds on. In MATHia, practice targets the skills not yet mastered inside the work the teacher assigns, and the teacher decides what comes next [1].

reasons.title: Continuous review
reasons.body: In AMP, learned skills come back in ordinary practice, at growing intervals, mixed with other math. In the MATHia course that was studied, students advanced as they mastered skills [7]. We found no scheduled return of mastered skills in the MATHia pages we read [1][2]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, practice that mixed and spaced topics scored 62% a month later on the researchers' own test, against 38% for practice in blocks [11].

reasons.title: A level for each part of math
reasons.body: AMP keeps a separate level for each part of math, on one map of skills from counting through precalculus. A learner further along in one part than another gets work at both levels. MATHia covers grades 6 to 12, from middle-school math through Algebra I, Geometry, Algebra II and Integrated Math I to III [2]. Kindergarten to grade 5 is a separate, game-based product, MATHia Adventure [3].

rows.range: Grades 6 to 12, by course, through Algebra II and Integrated Math III [2]. Kindergarten to grade 5 is a separate game-based product, MATHia Adventure [3].
rows.start: None found in the pages we read [1][2]. The teacher assigns the work [1].
rows.teaching: Problem solving with hints that respond to the student's strategy, checked step by step [1]. In the studied course, a teacher and textbook carried the lessons [7].
rows.next: Practice on skills not yet mastered, inside the work the teacher assigns. The teacher decides what comes next [1].
rows.mastery: In the studied course, students moved on as they mastered skills. A Skillometer shows progress skill by skill [1][7].
rows.review: None found in the pages we read [1][2].
rows.print: Student textbooks and worksheets in the blended course [7].
rows.adult: A teacher assigns the work, watches who is working or idle, and decides what comes next [1][2].
rows.reports: For teachers: a live view of who is working, skill-by-skill progress toward mastery, and projected outcomes [1][2].
rows.evidence: Blended Algebra I course: randomized trial, no effect in year one, about 0.2 SD in year two in high schools [5]. MATHia alone: unrated by Evidence for ESSA [9].

theirs: MATHia comes from Carnegie Learning, a Pittsburgh company [1]. It is tutoring software for grades 6 to 12, from middle-school math through Algebra I, Geometry, Algebra II and Integrated Math I to III [2]. Carnegie Learning describes it as working alongside core instruction, not replacing it [1]. A separate product, MATHia Adventure, offers game-based practice for kindergarten to grade 5 [3].

A student works through workspaces of real problems. MATHia responds to each step of the student's reasoning, not only the final answer, and its hints respond to the student's strategy [1]. Practice targets the skills the student has not yet mastered, and a Skillometer shows progress. The teacher assigns the work and decides what comes next [1][2].
credit: Step-by-step tutoring. MATHia follows each step of a student's reasoning, and its hints respond to the student's strategy [1].
Practice aimed at the skills a student has not yet mastered [1].
A large randomized trial of its earlier blended Algebra I course, run by RAND researchers [5].

theirs: MATHia's strongest evidence comes from Cognitive Tutor Algebra I, Carnegie Learning's earlier blended course, in which classes spent three days a week with a teacher and textbook and two on the software [7]. RAND researchers matched schools into pairs in seven states, randomly assigned one school in each pair to the course, and followed them for two years. The U.S. Institute of Education Sciences sponsored the trial's cost analysis [5][8]. In high schools the trial covered 73 schools in 51 districts and more than 11,000 students, against the schools' usual textbooks, with an algebra exam as the outcome [7]. There was no effect in the first year. In the second year high schools gained about 0.2 standard deviations, roughly 8 percentile points for the median student [5][6]. The middle-school estimate was similar in size but not significant [6].

The What Works Clearinghouse, using its own calculations, found no significant effect in year one and a year-two gain that lost significance after adjusting for multiple comparisons. It noted that students enrolled several months after schools were assigned. Its 2016 report on Cognitive Tutor Algebra I covered five studies with algebra findings, with an average gain of 4 percentile points and a range from -7 to +19. For Cognitive Tutor Geometry, one randomized study of 669 students, it found potentially negative effects, -8 points [7].

Evidence for ESSA rates Carnegie Learning's High School Math Solution Algebra I, which pairs MATHia with the curriculum, Strong, on three Cognitive Tutor Algebra I studies with an average effect size of +0.04 [10]. It lists MATHia on its own without a rating: "Qualifying studies found no significant positive outcomes" [9]. Carnegie Learning's research page says standalone MATHia meets ESSA Tier 2, and says the blended course "nearly doubled growth" in year two, which is the second-year result of the same trial [4]. It also cites EMERALDS, in which students who completed more MATHia workspaces in middle school did better in Algebra I [1][4]. That compares heavier users with lighter ones, and students who use a program most differ from the rest before they start.
ours: Two findings bear most on this comparison. In a randomized trial of 787 seventh graders that meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations, practice that mixed and spaced topics scored 62% a month later on the researchers' own test, against 38% for practice in blocks [11]. A meta-analysis of 55 studies found that worked examples improve math performance [12]. AMP applies both at every problem.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and AMP is open source.

them: You teach middle or high school math and want software that follows each step of a multistep problem, beside your own lessons.
amp: You want assessment, teaching and review in the same practice, with every answer setting the next problem.
You want a hint, a lesson and the worked answer at every problem, so no adult has to teach first.
You want learned skills to keep coming back in practice.
Your learner is at different levels in different parts of math, anywhere from counting to precalculus.

questions.question: How is AMP different from MATHia?
questions.answer: MATHia tutors each step of a problem inside workspaces a teacher assigns, and the teacher decides what comes next [1]. In AMP, every answer sets the next problem, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does MATHia work?
questions.answer: In a large randomized trial of its blended Cognitive Tutor Algebra I course, there was no effect in the first year and about 0.2 standard deviations in the second, in high schools [5]. Evidence for ESSA rates the blended High School Math Solution Algebra I Strong and lists MATHia on its own without a rating [10][9].

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. AMP is a separate program. It places a learner from their first answers, whatever they use at school.
